explanations.explanation: A mocker, friend. Solomon sets him next to the wise son: the son heeds his father's discipline, but a mocker does not listen to rebuke (Proverbs 13:1). Correction goes in one ear of that guy and out the other, probably with a joke on the way. I love a good joke, but I try to take the correction first.

Servants are a fine bunch, but they aren't in this line. Solomon's matchup is a wise son against a mocker, and it's the mocker who does not listen to rebuke (Proverbs 13:1). The wise son, meanwhile, heeds his father's discipline. Keep your eyes on that pair.

A stranger would be hard to rebuke, since nobody even knows his name. Fun thought, but Solomon says it's a mocker who does not listen to rebuke (Proverbs 13:1). The wise son sits on the other side of the matchup, heeding his father's discipline. This verse is family business, not a visitor at the door.

Peace would be nice, wouldn't it? But Solomon says the desire of the faithless is violence (Proverbs 13:2). On the other side of the matchup, a man enjoys good things from the fruit of his lips. Those two are reaching for very different things.

False it is, baker. The text says the desire of the faithless is violence, not peace (Proverbs 13:2). Across from that, a man enjoys good things from the fruit of his lips. Violence is not exactly a cookie swap kind of wanting.

Guarding his mouth, yes. Solomon says he who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin (Proverbs 13:3). Every adult has hit send on a reply-all and then stared at the screen wishing for a way to pull it back. A guarded mouth skips that whole feeling.

Gold is a fine thing to keep an eye on, but that's not what this line says. Solomon says it's he who guards his mouth who protects his life (Proverbs 13:3). Plenty of people lock the safe and leave the mouth wide open. The other man opens his lips and invites his own ruin.

Locking the doors is smart, but Solomon points somewhere closer. He who guards his mouth protects his life (Proverbs 13:3). Doors keep out the neighbors, but this guard post sits right under your nose. The one who opens his lips invites his own ruin.

Satisfied, baker. The slacker craves yet has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied (Proverbs 13:4). Both men want something, and only one of them rolls up his sleeves. Two lumps of dough can both dream of being cookies, but only the one that goes in the oven gets there.

Restless sounds close, since the slacker is the one craving. But Solomon puts the diligent on the satisfied side, where the soul is fully satisfied (Proverbs 13:4). It's the slacker who craves yet has nothing. Craving on one side, satisfaction on the other.

Ignored never shows up in this line. Solomon says the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied, while the slacker craves yet has nothing (Proverbs 13:4). Nobody's getting left out here, just two different results. The word to hold onto is satisfied, and he says fully.

It undermines him. Solomon says righteousness guards the man of integrity, but wickedness undermines the sinner (Proverbs 13:6). Picture a guy digging under his own porch, friend, and then wondering why the porch is shaky. One word guards, and the other digs from below.

Protecting belongs to the other side of the matchup. Righteousness guards the man of integrity, but wickedness undermines the sinner (Proverbs 13:6). Same sentence, opposite jobs. Wickedness never gets the guard duty.

A promotion would be a nice surprise, but this isn't a raise. Solomon says wickedness undermines the sinner, while righteousness guards the man of integrity (Proverbs 13:6). There's no corner office on the wicked side of this line.

True. One pretends to be rich but has nothing, and another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth (Proverbs 13:7). It's a mirror-image pair, with both men acting out something they aren't. I'd tell you why each one does it, but the verse doesn't say, so I'll leave it right there.

It's true, friend, and that's the twist. Solomon says one pretends to be rich but has nothing, and another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth (Proverbs 13:7). Both men are acting, just in opposite directions. The verse doesn't tell us why, so I'm not going to guess.

No threat, baker. Solomon says riches may ransom a man's life, but a poor man hears no threat (Proverbs 13:8). It's one short line with two men in it, and I'm not going to make up a story to explain it, since the verse doesn't give one. I'll just say Solomon packs a lot into one verse.

Praise sounds like a nicer thing to hear, I'll give you that. But the verse says a poor man hears no threat (Proverbs 13:8). Riches may ransom a man's life, and that's the other half of the pair. No compliments in this one, friend.

Music would make this verse a lot more fun, but it isn't there. Solomon says a poor man hears no threat, while riches may ransom a man's life (Proverbs 13:8). No band, no playlist, no threat. Just the one thing the verse names.

That lamp doesn't keep burning, friend. Solomon says the light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished (Proverbs 13:9). One light is bright, and the other one goes out. If you ever have to pick a side of this matchup, pick the side with the light on.

False, and the verse is plain about it. The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished (Proverbs 13:9). Bright on one side, put out on the other. Not much flickering in between.

Advice, baker. Solomon says arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised (Proverbs 13:10). A well-advised person has let others weigh in. I ask folks all the time how long to chill the dough, and my cookies thank me.

Credit is something arrogance loves to grab, but it isn't what this verse says. Solomon says wisdom is with the well-advised (Proverbs 13:10). Arrogance leads only to strife. The well-advised are the ones who take in what others tell them.

Shortcuts never come up in this verse. Solomon says arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised (Proverbs 13:10). The word that fits the blank is advice. Skipping steps in my bakery gets you a flat cookie and a very confused apron.

Dwindle, friend. Solomon says dishonest wealth will dwindle, but what is earned through hard work will be multiplied (Proverbs 13:11). It's like a cookie box with a sneaky hand reaching in, and every time you look there's less. The hard-earned pile heads the other way.

Endure is a good word, but Solomon doesn't put it on dishonest wealth. He says it will dwindle, while what is earned through hard work will be multiplied (Proverbs 13:11). One pile shrinks and the other multiplies. Quite a difference between the two.

Double is on the right track for the other pile, but not this one. Solomon says what is earned through hard work will be multiplied, and dishonest wealth will dwindle (Proverbs 13:11). Dwindle means it gets smaller, friend. That's the opposite of a double batch.

True, baker. Solomon says desire fulfilled is a tree of life (Proverbs 13:12). Right before it comes the hard part, where hope deferred makes the heart sick. So the verse holds both the long wait and the good thing that finally arrives. I think that arrival feels like a warm batch coming out of the oven.

That one is true, friend. The verse says hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life (Proverbs 13:12). A sick heart on one side, a tree of life on the other. Quite a swing, and I think the second one is worth the wait.

True. Solomon says he who despises instruction will pay the penalty, but the one who respects a command will be rewarded (Proverbs 13:13). That's the whole matchup in one verse: a penalty on one side, a reward on the other. I'll admit I've been on both sides of a recipe card.

It's true, baker. The verse says the one who respects a command will be rewarded (Proverbs 13:13). The penalty belongs to the one who despises instruction. Reward on one side, penalty on the other, and I'd pick respect every time.

The snares of death. Solomon says the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death (Proverbs 13:14). A snare is a trap. Picture a trap hidden in the tall grass, with a sign pointing you around it, and the teaching is the sign.

A house of mourning is a solemn picture, but it isn't in this verse. Solomon says the teaching of the wise turns one from the snares of death (Proverbs 13:14). A snare is a trap. And the teaching itself is a fountain of life.

The sea never comes up in this verse, friend. Solomon says the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death (Proverbs 13:14). A snare is a trap, so this is about being turned away from one. My cookie planet has no sea, so I'm keeping my feet dry on this one.

Folly kept hidden would be nice for the fool, but that's not what Solomon says. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool displays his folly (Proverbs 13:16). Displays means it's out in the open, like a sign hung on the front of the bakery. Nobody has to go looking for it.

False, baker. Solomon says every prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool displays his folly (Proverbs 13:16). That folly is out where everybody can see it, like a stain on the front of a shirt. I've worn that shirt, friend, with flour all down the apron, and it was not easy to hide.

Healing, friend. Solomon says a wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing (Proverbs 13:17). An envoy is someone sent with a message. I think that's the kind of delivery everybody hopes for.

Delay is what you'd expect from a slow mail truck, but Solomon doesn't say it. He says a wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing (Proverbs 13:17). Healing is the word, and it's a good one. No late notices attached.

Confusion sounds like a group chat with forty replies at once, but it isn't in the verse. Solomon says a faithful envoy brings healing, while a wicked messenger falls into trouble (Proverbs 13:17). The envoy's side ends on healing. That's a lot nicer to hand a person than confusion.

Honored, baker. Solomon says poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored (Proverbs 13:18). Correction can sting a little going in. I've pressed some crooked cookies in my day, and every one taught me something.

Ashamed is what the verse says about the other side. Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored (Proverbs 13:18). It's an easy pair to swap, friend, so no worries. The one who heeds is the one who's honored.

Forgotten isn't in this line at all. Solomon says whoever heeds correction is honored (Proverbs 13:18). Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline. Honor for one, poverty and shame for the other.

Turning from evil, yes. Solomon says desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but turning from evil is detestable to fools (Proverbs 13:19). It starts sweet, and then the line swings the other way. I'd call that a plot twist, but it's a proverb.

Waiting their turn is a very polite guess, and I'd give it points at any bakery counter. But Solomon says turning from evil is detestable to fools (Proverbs 13:19). Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, the verse says, and then it flips to the other side.

Working the fields is honest labor, and it isn't what this verse names. Solomon says turning from evil is detestable to fools (Proverbs 13:19). Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, and then the line swings to the other side. Fields don't come into it.

He will be destroyed, friend. Solomon says he who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed (Proverbs 13:20). The company you keep is a big deal in this verse. I'd rather follow somebody who knows the way to the oven.

Growing rich is a nice dream, but it isn't what Solomon says. The companion of fools will be destroyed (Proverbs 13:20). The one who walks with the wise will become wise. That's the pair, and money isn't in it.

Envied would at least be flattering, but nobody's sending the companion of fools a thank-you card. Solomon says he will be destroyed (Proverbs 13:20). The one who walks with the wise will become wise. That's a serious contrast, so I'll let the verse stand as written.

True. Solomon says disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous (Proverbs 13:21). One gets chased and the other gets rewarded. Nobody wants to be the one getting chased, friend. I'd sooner be sitting in the bakery with a warm batch.

It's true, friend. The verse says disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous (Proverbs 13:21). Disaster on one side, prosperity on the other. If the second half sounded too good to be in there, I get it, but that's what Solomon wrote.

The righteous, baker. Solomon says a good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children, but the sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous (Proverbs 13:22). That wealth changes hands. It's like a cookie jar sliding all the way down the counter to somebody else.

Neighbors are a friendly guess, but Solomon names someone else. The sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous (Proverbs 13:22). Right before that, a good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children. The neighbors might get a wave, but no wealth from this verse.

Priests aren't named in this verse. Solomon says the sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous (Proverbs 13:22). The first half of the line is about a good man leaving an inheritance to his children's children. The righteous are the ones the verse points to.

A lack of justice. Solomon says abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away (Proverbs 13:23). There was plenty there, and it still got swept away. I think this one hurts a little.

Rain is a fair guess, since food and ground go together. But the verse says without justice it is swept away (Proverbs 13:23). The abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor. Justice is the missing piece Solomon names.

Locusts would be a dramatic way to lose a harvest, but they aren't in this verse. Solomon says abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away (Proverbs 13:23). The missing piece is justice. I think that makes it a quieter line, but a heavy one.

Disciplines, friend. Solomon says he who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently (Proverbs 13:24). He sets love and discipline together in this one. It's a weighty line, so it's worth reading slowly.

Excuses are a gentle guess, but the verse says something else. He who loves his son disciplines him diligently (Proverbs 13:24). It's the one who spares the rod that Solomon says hates his son. Those are Solomon's words, so I'll leave them as written.

Spoils is a clever pick, but it isn't in the verse. Solomon says he who loves his son disciplines him diligently (Proverbs 13:24). The one who spares the rod gets the harder word, hates. I'll let the verse speak for itself.

A full stomach for the wicked is the opposite of what the verse says. Solomon says a righteous man eats to his heart's content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty (Proverbs 13:25). So it's content on one side and empty on the other. Meanwhile I'm loosening my apron strings just thinking about the content part.

False, baker. Solomon says a righteous man eats to his heart's content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty (Proverbs 13:25). Eating to your heart's content is my kind of ending for a chapter. I'd have to let out the apron strings, but I'd do it gladly.
